signals.title: DS@GT ARC at CheckThat! 2026: A Verdict-Anchored Pipeline for Generating Fact-Checking Articles
signals.summary: Misinformation spreads faster than professional fact-checkers can manually verify it and write articles explaining their verdicts. This creates a need to automate the production of fact-checking articles.
signals.implication: High relevance to C2A2 operations; include in next leadership brief.
signals.long_summary: Misinformation is proliferating at a pace that exceeds the ability of professional fact-checkers to manually verify claims and produce explanatory articles. This highlights a pressing need for automation in the creation of fact-checking content. The item discusses the development of a method aimed at addressing this gap by generating fact-checking articles more efficiently. It emphasizes the importance of facilitating timely responses to misinformation through automated systems. This matters for a community keeping up with AI, as understanding advancements in automated fact-checking can enhance media literacy and help combat the spread of false information.

signals.title: Agent Harness Awareness: Turning Verified Telemetry into Operational Control for Tool-Using Agents
signals.summary: Tool descriptions tell an agent what an action can do, but they do not necessarily reveal whether that action is healthy or suitable at the moment of use. Execution harnesses often possess this information through monitors, traces, and recent failures while the model choosing the next action does not.
signals.implication: Reassess role boundaries and human override for community deployments. Update constitutional clauses and compliance mappings for community operators. High relevance to C2A2 operations; include in next leadership brief.
signals.long_summary: Tool descriptions provide agents with information on what actions can be performed but often lack insight into whether those actions are appropriate or safe at the time of execution. Execution harnesses are equipped with monitors, traces, and data on recent failures, which can inform the decision-making process of agents. This difference indicates a gap between available capabilities and the operational intelligence that can guide agents toward healthier choices. Understanding this distinction is vital for enhancing the operational control of tool-using agents. This matters for the community keeping up with AI as it highlights the need for improved governance and policy development around agent capabilities and their safe application in real-time scenarios.

signals.title: Information-Matched Auditing of Conversational Emotion-Shift Forecasting: A Leakage-Safe Evaluation Protocol
signals.summary: Comparisons in conversational emotion-shift forecasting are easily distorted when a learned model receives rich features but its transition baseline is given a noisy or unavailable current-emotion label, when hyperparameter budgets differ, or when target-turn information enters the representation. We present an information-matched, leakage-safe auditing protocol that closes these gaps with an explicit commitment point, executable causality tests, equal four-configuration validation searches, and seed-dialogue-aware inference.
signals.implication: Update constitutional clauses and compliance mappings for community operators.
signals.long_summary: The paper discusses issues in evaluating conversational emotion-shift forecasting models, particularly how their performance can be skewed by variables such as the quality of current-emotion labels, differing hyperparameter budgets, and the influence of target-turn information on model representations. To address these challenges, the authors propose an information-matched, leakage-safe auditing protocol. This protocol aims to enhance evaluation accuracy by implementing several strategies, including establishing a clear commitment point, conducting executable causality tests, and performing uniform validation searches across four configurations, along with seed-dialogue-aware inference. This development is significant for the AI community as it contributes to more reliable assessments of emotion forecasting models, which can impact user interactions and emotional engagement in conversational AI systems.

signals.title: TandemBench: Benchmarking Decision Models for Multi-Agent Collaboration
signals.summary: Decision models choose among predefined options in tasks such as routing and action selection. In multi-agent collaboration, a decision determines how members divide work, exchange resources, and act in parallel.
signals.implication: Reassess role boundaries and human override for community deployments.
signals.long_summary: Decision models are essential for selecting among predefined options in various tasks, including routing and action selection. In the context of multi-agent collaboration, these models play a critical role in how agents partition tasks, share resources, and coordinate their actions simultaneously. This research underscores the importance of decision-making frameworks in enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of collaborative efforts among multiple agents. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for the AI community, as it highlights how advancements in decision models can improve collaboration in complex AI systems.

signals.title: Learning When Human Decisions Matter: Executor-Relative Consultation Value for LLM Agents
signals.summary: Large language models increasingly automate complex tasks, but human decision capacity does not scale with their capabilities. In many applications, humans remain essential for providing private context, authority, or judgments unavailable to the agent.
signals.implication: Reassess role boundaries and human override for community deployments.
signals.long_summary: Large language models are advancing in their ability to automate complex tasks, yet the need for human input remains critical as their capability does not coincide with human decision-making capacity. In several applications, humans play an indispensable role by providing private context, authority, or judgments that the models are unable to access or replicate. This emphasizes the ongoing importance of human oversight and input in AI systems, highlighting that technology cannot fully replace the nuanced decision-making that humans provide. Understanding this dynamic is essential for a community engaged with AI, as it underscores the need for continued collaboration between human intelligence and machine capabilities.

signals.title: Phonological Knowledge of Chinese Characters in Language Models
signals.summary: How much phonological knowledge do language models (LMs) possess about Chinese characters, and how is this knowledge represented and used? We introduce PinyinBench, a controlled benchmark covering homophones, phonological features (initials, finals, and tones), and polyphonic characters.
signals.implication: Reassess role boundaries and human override for community deployments.
signals.long_summary: This research introduces PinyinBench, a benchmark designed to assess the phonological knowledge of language models in relation to Chinese characters. It focuses on various aspects such as homophones, phonological features including initials, finals, and tones, as well as polyphonic characters. The study aims to understand how language models represent and utilize this phonological knowledge. Given the growing importance of language models in processing diverse languages, including Chinese, this development is significant for communities aiming to enhance their understanding of how AI interprets phonological elements in language.

signals.title: Prospective Memory for Proactive LLM Agents
signals.summary: Most memory systems for LLM agents are retrospective, preserving and retrieving past information to inform current decisions. Proactive agents, however, also require prospective memory: retaining future-directed intentions and realizing them when appropriate opportunities arise, even without explicit requests.
signals.implication: Reassess role boundaries and human override for community deployments.
signals.long_summary: Most memory systems for language model (LLM) agents focus on retrospective memory, which involves preserving and retrieving past information to guide current decisions. However, proactive agents require a different approach known as prospective memory. This type of memory allows agents to retain intentions about future actions and to act upon them when suitable opportunities present themselves, even without explicit prompts to do so. This development highlights the importance of designing LLMs that can plan and execute future-oriented tasks effectively, expanding their capabilities beyond merely reacting to past interactions. Understanding these distinctions is crucial for a community that seeks to keep up with evolving AI technologies and their potential applications in various domains.

signals.title: SRRM: A Retrieval-Reconstruction Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Context Memory in Small Language Models
signals.summary: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed on consumer-grade hardware, yet their ability to preserve information across progressively longer contexts remains insufficiently understood. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate retrieval-oriented tasks, providing limited insight into whether successful retrieval reflects comprehensive long-context memory preservation.
signals.implication: Track for context; no immediate governance action required.
signals.long_summary: The abstract discusses the limitations of existing benchmarks for Small Language Models (SLMs), particularly regarding their performance in retaining information across longer contexts. While SLMs are used more frequently on consumer hardware, there is a lack of understanding about how effectively they manage long-context memory. Current benchmarks tend to focus mainly on retrieval tasks, which do not adequately represent the broader challenge of maintaining memory over extended contexts. This is significant for the community as it highlights the need for improved evaluation methods that better reflect the capabilities of SLMs in real-world applications where context retention is crucial.

signals.title: Human-like cross-language generalisation in deep neural speaker embeddings and its acoustic foundations
signals.summary: Generalisability is a central question for deep neural networks, including the cross-language generalisation of speaker embeddings. This study examined whether deep neural speaker embeddings generalise across languages and how such generalisation relates to human perception and acoustic structure.
signals.implication: Reassess role boundaries and human override for community deployments.
signals.long_summary: This study investigates the ability of deep neural speaker embeddings to generalize across different languages and explores how this generalization aligns with human perception and the acoustic characteristics of speech. The focus is on the generalizability aspect of neural networks, particularly in the context of speaker recognition across various linguistic contexts. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for improving AI's performance in multilingual representations and applications. This development is relevant for the community as it highlights advancements in language processing and AI's ability to bridge linguistic barriers.
